fr:frontmatter.fr:meta: @misc{yeCAKECompilerAgentCoDesign2026, title = {{{CAKE}}: {{Compiler-Agent Co-Design}} for {{Frontier Kernel Evolution}}}, author = {Ye, Zihao and Huang, Yingyi and Jin, Hongyi and Hou, Bohan and Shao, Junru and Yu, Zhongming and Chen, Jinqi and Cowan, Meghan and Cao, Shiyi and Xing, Shanli and Chen, Hanfeng and Grover, Vinod and Chen, Tianqi and Ceze, Luis}, year = {2026}, doi = {10.48550/ARXIV.2608.12629}, urldate = {2026-08-15}, publisher = {arXiv}, file = {/home/kellen/Downloads/papers/CAKE Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution - Ye et al..pdf}, keywords = {FOS: Computer and information sciences,Machine Learning (cs.LG)}, copyright = {arXiv.org perpetual, non-exclusive license}, abstract = {Work on GPU kernel agents and work on GPU programming languages have advanced separately, and the gap between them is where expert kernels are lost. Kernel agents treat the compiler as a fixed black box: they improve proposal, mutation, and ranking, but the environment returns only compiler errors, correctness outcomes, and end-to-end timing---signals that never say which program decision caused a synchronization failure, a hardware-contract violation, or a pipeline stall, and that cannot grow when a frontier workload exposes a missing capability. Meanwhile the languages an agent might write are not built for one. Tile-level DSLs hide the warp specialization, barrier choreography, and memory-tier placement that separate expert kernels from merely correct ones; low-level DSLs expose that control but demand a layout calculus that makes agent errors both likely and hard to localize. We present Cake, which codesigns the two. Agents author Cake IR, a typed, hardware-explicit schedule representation that gives fine-grained control without a layout algebra and carries enough information for a verifier and cost model to reason about a program before it is compiled; the harness answers with localized correctness and performance diagnostics and is itself a target of evolution, so recurring failures become new verifier rules, IR primitives, cost-model calibrations, and reusable tactics rather than one-off workarounds. Across matched implementation-hidden Flash-KMeans clean starts on B200 (three runs per representation), the best candidate at an 80-million-token budget reaches a median 1.144\texttimes{} the tuned FlashML baseline with Cake IR, versus 0.928\texttimes{} for direct CUDA/PTX. Beyond the clean-start benchmark, agent-generated Kimi Delta Attention reaches a 2.05\texttimes{} geometric-mean speedup over official FlashKDA and is validated in end-to-end serving. Dispatcher-backed KNN and KMeans families improve performance by 1.42\texttimes --2.12\texttimes{} across more than 400 shapes, and four kernel changes are available as upstream PRs. Cake targets NVIDIA GPUs from Ampere through Blackwell and separates single-shape evolution from the generalization and dispatch stage required for library integration.}, month = {August}, shorttitle = {{{CAKE}}} }

fr:title.text: POTW: 🎂 CAKE: Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: POTW: 🎂 CAKE: Compiler-Agent Co-Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Problem. In this paper, they aim to address the problem of agentic kernel generation or as we refer to it: vibe compilation. Specifically, they target CUDA and raw PTX as a backend.
Technical challenges. There are many issues that arise in vibe compilation. A non-exhaustive list of challenges is as follows:

html:ul.html:li: Reward Hacking: A very common theme for any reinforcement learning based approach. In particular, see this paper for some examples of agents hacking KernelBench.

Synchronization errors: Even given a list of input output examples to check against, we cannot possibly determine whether there is an underlying race condition that appears rarely enough to pass the checks.
This seems to be a main focus of things like TIRx, where they hope to check these things at the IR level.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Core contribution. They develop CAKE IR, which is an intermediate representation for writing CUDA kernels. More importantly, they have the agent co-design the IR while trying to generate kernels. This is an iterative process, where the agent must implement existing kernels in its own designed IR. To do so, requires adding necessary features to the IR like Warp Specialization along with the corresponding lowering passes.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Starting bare IR. The agent is then given a warp-specialized kernel and sees that it needs to add support for warp specialization via lm.role

fr:mainmatter.html:p: They can then iteratively build on this pipeline adding architecture specific features. For example, the IR example they give shows that they have an lm.tmem API for TMEM. This can be thought of as a v3 given below.

html:figure.html:figcaption: Building on the IR with Warp Specialization. Add support for architecture specific features like TMEM as the candles on top of the IR

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How this is actually implemented is a trade secretI suspect one reason that a lot of this is not publicly available is that it is only understood by GPT 5.6.
Evaluation. They evaluate against (their own) well-tuned kernels from FlashInfer.

Where they might struggle. It is unclear how well this would work for ASICs like TPUs or Trainium. I suspect that in order to "converge" to a good IR, you need to reduce the degrees of freedom through a large number of kernel examples. The kernel ecosystem of these accelerators is far less mature, making it much harder to extract useful abstractions.
I believe the layering analogy was meant as adding increasingly specific features, but I wonder whether a vibe MLIR could be developed to allow other accelerators to inherit some of the benefits.
Most of the work in this paper is not publicly available, so I have a lot of outstanding questions.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. What are the exact input / outputs in IR developement and during search?
fr:mainmatter.html:p: For the IR, they have "IR principles"

My best guess is that the workflow is roughly 1. prepend these principles to the input via some prompt 2. provide new kernel(s) that likely require some new abstraction and 3. have GPT vibe code IR updates.

Additionally, my post-lunch block is very ineffective. I had the genius idea of eliminating the cognitive overhead of organizing and transferring notes by deferring until the afternoon block. In the morning block, I will just dump everything I might care about later. Then, in the later block, I will do the menial, low cognitive demand task of choosing what stays and where it goes. This can also serve as a form of review.
